screens.title: SD-Access Underlay Network Design & Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why a robust Layer 3 underlay is the foundation of any SD-Access fabric. The underlay is the IP transport that provides reachability between fabric edge, border, and control-plane nodes. You will see how routed access avoids spanning tree, how loopback addresses act as stable RLOCs for the overlay, and why choosing and configuring your underlay routing protocol correctly matters for scale and convergence. For example, assigning contiguous /32 loopbacks simplifies Router ID selection and route distribution, while using point-to-point links reduces OSPF complexity and speeds convergence. We will also show the CLI steps to configure loopbacks and OSPF and demonstrate verification commands that confirm your underlay is healthy. A common misconception is that overlay technologies can compensate for a poor underlay — they cannot; the overlay depends entirely on full IP reachability. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design loopback and link addressing, select and configure an underlay protocol, verify end-to-end RLOC reachability, and recognize configuration mistakes that break reachability. Takeaway: a well-designed underlay prevents many later troubleshooting headaches in the overlay.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives will guide your hands-on work with an SD-Access underlay. First, you'll design an IP addressing scheme that separates loopbacks from point-to-point link subnets and follows best practice allocations so RLOCs remain stable. For example, reserving a /24 or larger contiguous block for loopbacks and using /30 links avoids address overlap and improves troubleshooting. Second, you'll configure a robust underlay routing protocol—OSPF, EIGRP, or ISIS—ensuring full reachability of loopback RLOCs. Knowing when to pick OSPF versus ISIS matters in scaling. Third, you'll implement routed access by extending Layer 3 to the access edge, which removes spanning tree complexity and shortens convergence. Finally, you'll learn to identify common pitfalls such as inconsistent area IDs, missing loopback advertisements, and accidentally extending Layer 2 across fabric edge nodes. Each objective includes verification steps and an example so you can practice with confidence.

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical verification and the small design details that prevent outages. You will learn to verify underlay connectivity using OSPF neighbor tables, routing tables, pings to loopback addresses, and traceroutes to confirm forwarding paths. Each objective is paired with practical CLI steps so you can test and validate during hands-on labs. screens.title: What the Underlay Is and Why It Matters
screens.narratorSegment: The underlay is the IP transport network that connects all fabric-enabled devices and provides the basic reachability the overlay requires. In SD-Access the underlay should be routed: that means every physical link between switches and routers is a Layer 3 point-to-point connection, and there is no Layer 2 stretching across multiple fabric edge nodes. Concretely, the underlay carries routes to the loopback addresses of every device, which act as RLOCs for the LISP overlay. A practical example: if an access switch needs to reach the control-plane node, it uses the underlay routes to the control-plane loopback IP. A common misconception is that overlay smartness replaces a solid underlay; it does not. The overlay relies on the underlay for IP reachability, and problems in the underlay show up as broken overlay services. Key reasons the underlay matters include faster convergence from routed access, elimination of STP limitations, and localized failure domains that reduce outage scope. When designing the underlay, plan addressing, choose an appropriate routing protocol, and confirm loopbacks and point-to-point links are advertised. Reflect: before touching the overlay, can you verify that every loopback is reachable from every fabric node?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: An IP-based routed transport that supplies reachability for overlay RLOCs and removes Layer 2 scaling limits.

content.html:
Core Concept
What the underlay is
The routed IP transport that provides stable reachability for all fabric nodes and their loopbacks.
Role
Transports packets between fabric edge, border, and control nodes using Layer 3 routing.
Why it matters
Overlay functions like segmentation and LISP rely on the underlay for RLOC reachability; without it the overlay cannot operate.
Common misconception
Thinking overlay resiliency replaces underlay correctness. The underlay must be healthy first.
Concrete example
An access switch's loopback and a control-plane node loopback must be present in the underlay routing table so that packets reach the correct device for overlay control-plane communication.
Check your understanding
Can you list the three device types that must be reachable over the underlay: Fabric Edge, Fabric Border, Fabric Control Plane?
Key Takeaway

Treat the underlay as the single source of truth for IP reachability before deploying the overlay.

screens.title: Routed Access vs Layer 2 Extension
screens.narratorSegment: Routed access and Layer 2 extension represent two very different underlay philosophies. Routed access extends Layer 3 to the access edge and treats each link as a point-to-point routed segment; Layer 2 extension stretches VLANs across devices and depends on Spanning Tree Protocol. Routed access is recommended for SD-Access because it eliminates STP complexity, localizes failure domains, and allows faster convergence. For example, if a link fails in a routed access design, only that subnet and adjacent routes reconverge, whereas a Layer 2 domain can trigger broader STP recalculations and longer reconvergence windows. A common mistake is attempting to maintain stretched VLANs to preserve legacy behavior; this reintroduces STP and undermines the overlay's separation of forwarding and control. The benefit in practice is stable, predictable underlay behavior that the overlay can depend on. Consider a campus where hundreds of access switches exist: routed access prevents a single broadcast domain from ballooning and causing widespread instability. Question to reflect on: if you inherit a network with VLANs stretched across access nodes, what steps will you take to migrate to routed access safely?

keyIdea.title: Why routed access
keyIdea.text: Routed access reduces STP dependence, improves convergence, and keeps failure domains small — essential for scalable SD-Access.

content.html:
Comparison
Routed Access vs Layer 2 Extension
Routed Access
  • Layer 3 to the access edge
  • No STP across fabric edges
  • Faster convergence
Layer 2 Extension
  • VLANs span multiple switches
  • Relies on STP for loop prevention
  • Wider failure domains
Misconception
Keeping Layer 2 stretches 'for convenience' reintroduces old problems and should be avoided in new SD-Access underlays.
Concrete scenario
In a campus migration, convert access switch ports from access VLANs spanning multiple nodes to routed access interfaces, then move segmentation into the overlay, avoiding STP-wide reconvergence during topology changes.
Key Takeaway

Adopt routed access to prevent STP complexity and ensure predictable underlay convergence.

Reflective question: What migration steps would you plan to move from VLAN stretching to routed access in a live campus?

screens.title: Designing an IP Addressing Scheme for the Underlay
screens.narratorSegment: A deliberate IP addressing plan makes an SD-Access underlay manageable and scalable. Start by reserving a contiguous block for loopback interfaces — for example a /24 or /22 depending on fabric size — and assign /32 addresses to each device's loopback. These loopbacks become the RLOCs used by the overlay, and using contiguous addresses simplifies summarization and documentation. Next, allocate small subnets for point-to-point links, typically /30 or /31; these conserve address space and clearly indicate link endpoints. Where supported, you can use unnumbered interfaces to avoid wasting addresses, but be consistent and document the approach. A typical process: 1) Estimate number of fabric devices and select loopback block size; 2) Reserve a separate block for P2P links; 3) Assign static /32 loopbacks and small P2P subnets; 4) Update routing protocol advertisements and verify. Example: use 10.255.255.0/24 for loopbacks with 10.255.255.1 and.2 as device /32s, and 192.168.10.0/30 for a specific link. Misconception to avoid: using large shared subnets for access links that blur routing boundaries. The core question: does your address plan make it trivial to locate which subnet belongs to which link or device?

keyIdea.title: Addressing process
keyIdea.text: Reserve contiguous loopback space and small P2P subnets so RLOCs and links are clear and easily verified.

content.html:
Process Flow
Underlay addressing steps
  1. Estimate device count and reserve a contiguous block for loopbacks (e.g., /24 or /22).
  2. Assign each loopback a /32 and use those as RLOCs and Router IDs.
  3. Allocate small subnets (/30 or /31) for each point-to-point link.
  4. Document and advertise loopbacks and links in your routing protocol.
Why contiguous loopbacks?
Contiguous ranges allow easier route filtering, summarization, and quick identification of RLOCs in routing tables.
Concrete example
Loopback pool: 10.255.255.0/24; assign 10.255.255.1/32 to FabricEdge1 and 10.255.255.2/32 to FabricBorder1. Point-to-point link: 192.168.10.0/30 with .1 and .2 for the two endpoints.
interface Loopback0
 ip address 10.255.255.1 255.255.255.255
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 no switchport
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf network point-to-point
Key Takeaway

A clear addressing plan makes troubleshooting and scaling the underlay much easier.

screens.title: Loopback Interfaces and RLOCs
screens.narratorSegment: Loopback interfaces are virtual interfaces with a stable, always-up IP address, and in SD-Access they serve two critical roles. First, a loopback often becomes the Router ID for your routing protocol, ensuring a consistent identity even as physical interfaces flap. Second, loopback addresses serve as RLOCs — LISP Routing Locators — in the overlay control plane so that the overlay maps endpoints to physical devices. Best practice is to place loopbacks into a dedicated contiguous subnet and assign each device a /32. For instance, using 10.255.255.0/24 for all loopbacks and giving FabricEdge1 10.255.255.1/32 guarantees predictability. A common pitfall is failing to advertise loopbacks into the underlay routing protocol; if a loopback isn't advertised, other fabric nodes cannot reach that RLOC and overlay control fails. Verification steps include checking the routing table for the loopback prefixes and pinging other devices' loopbacks. Quick check: if your router-id is an interface address that can go down, you risk losing consistent routing identity — prefer loopbacks for stability. Loopback Interfaces and RLOCs means use /32 loopbacks from a dedicated block as stable router ids and rlocs; always advertise them into the underlay.. In practical terms, why loopbacks are stable identifiers for fabric devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Loopback role
keyIdea.text: Use /32 loopbacks from a dedicated block as stable Router IDs and RLOCs; always advertise them into the underlay.

content.html:
Definition
Loopbacks & RLOCs
Stable, always-up addresses used as Router IDs and overlay RLOCs; assign /32s from a contiguous block.
Why /32?
/32 loopbacks avoid ambiguity and ensure the address is unique to one device for RLOC mapping.
Pitfall
Forgetting to advertise the loopback into the routing protocol removes reachability for RLOCs.
Configuration snippet
interface Loopback0
 ip address 10.255.255.1 255.255.255.255
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 10.255.255.1
 network 10.255.255.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
Key Takeaway

Loopbacks are reliable anchors for both routing and overlay mapping—advertise them always.

screens.title: Point-to-Point Links and OSPF Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: Point-to-point links are a fundamental underlay construct. They connect two devices directly and should be configured as Layer 3 links with their own small subnets to avoid shared broadcast domains. Typical choices are /30 subnets, which give two usable addresses, or /31 subnets when supported, which are even more address-efficient. Where you cannot or prefer not to assign an address, unnumbered interfaces are an option. In OSPF, apply the ip ospf network point-to-point command to these links so that the protocol does not perform DR/BDR elections, which are unnecessary for two-party links and can slow convergence. Example: configuring GigabitEthernet1/0/1 with 192.168.10.1/30 and setting ip ospf network point-to-point tells OSPF this is a direct link, which streamlines adjacency formation. Misconception to avoid: using larger subnets like /24 for point-to-point links wastes address space and may confuse topology reasoning. Key verification: ensure that the link's subnet and the OSPF interface type are both correct so the adjacency forms cleanly. Point-to-Point Links and OSPF Optimization means use /30 or /31 subnets for point-to-point links and set ospf to point-to-point to avoid dr/bdr delays.. In practical terms, choose the right subnet sizes and ospf interface type. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Point-to-Point Links
Direct Layer 3 links between two devices; use small subnets and OSPF point-to-point mode for efficiency.
Recommended subnets
/30 or /31; choose /31 when supported to save addresses.
OSPF optimization
Use the ip ospf network point-to-point command to avoid DR/BDR elections on P2P links.
Configuration example
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 no switchport
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.252

Key Takeaway

Small P2P subnets and the OSPF point-to-point type reduce protocol overhead and accelerate convergence.

screens.title: Selecting an Underlay Routing Protocol
screens.narratorSegment: Three common choices for the SD-Access underlay are OSPF, EIGRP, and ISIS. OSPF is widely understood, supports multi-area designs, and is suitable for many sized fabrics. EIGRP can be simpler in some Cisco-centric environments, while ISIS is often preferred in very large deployments because of its scalability, efficient summarization, and native multi-topology capabilities. The key requirement, regardless of choice, is full reachability between all loopback RLOCs. For example, in a small campus you might use OSPF in a single area for simplicity; in a large, multi-site fabric, ISIS may reduce operational overhead and scale better. A common misconception is that one protocol will magically eliminate design flaws — protocol choice cannot compensate for poor addressing or missing loopback advertisements. When deciding, weigh the team's operational familiarity, scale needs, summarization requirements, and multi-topology needs. Final reflection: which protocol matches your environment's scale and your team's operational expertise? Selecting an Underlay Routing Protocol means choose the routing protocol that meets your scale, summarization, and operational familiarity while ensuring full rloc reachability.. In practical terms, ospf, eigrp, and isis — tradeoffs and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: OSPF Underlay Configuration Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a compact OSPF underlay configuration for a fabric edge node. The example shows creating a loopback with a /32 address, configuring a routed GigabitEthernet interface for the point-to-point link, and enabling OSPF with a router ID matching the loopback. The loopback provides a stable Router ID and RLOC. The point-to-point interface uses a /30 and the command ip ospf network point-to-point to prevent DR/BDR elections. Code Walkthrough
OSPF underlay snippet
// FabricEdge1 configuration
hostname FabricEdge1
!
interface Loopback0

!

screens.title: Verify Underlay Connectivity and Routing
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is a step you must complete before deploying the overlay. Start by confirming OSPF adjacency with show ip ospf neighbor; a full adjacency indicates the two routers have exchanged LSAs successfully. Next, inspect the routing table with show ip route ospf to confirm that loopback /32s and point-to-point networks appear as OSPF-learned routes. Use ping to test reachability to every other device's loopback RLOC; successful pings mean the underlay can carry overlay control-plane traffic. Traceroute helps you validate the forwarding path and detect unexpected hops or route redistribution issues. X. A frequent root cause of failed pings is an unadvertised loopback. If a loopback is missing from the routing table, verify the network statement in the router OSPF configuration. screens.title: Common Underlay Design and Configuration Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes cause underlay failures. First, extending Layer 2 across fabric edge nodes undermines routed access and reintroduces STP issues. Avoid this by migrating ports to routed interfaces and performing the overlay segmentation in software. Second, inconsistent routing protocol settings — such as wrong OSPF area IDs or incorrect EIGRP AS numbers — can prevent full adjacency or route propagation. Always standardize process IDs and area numbers in your design documents. Third, failing to advertise loopbacks into the routing process is a frequent source of missing RLOCs; verify network statements or redistribution policies. Fourth, careless addressing, such as using large shared subnets for links, can make it hard to determine endpoints and invite mistakes. Mitigation strategies include documenting address plans, applying configuration templates, performing changes in maintenance windows, and validating with show commands before overlay deployment. A useful practice is a pre-overlay checklist: verify loopback advertisements, confirm OSPF neighbors are Full, and ping every loopback from multiple nodes. Closing question: do you have automated checks or scripts to confirm these items before you enable overlay services? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why a robust Layer 3 underlay is the foundation of any SD-Access fabric. The underlay is the IP transport that provides reachability between fabric edge, border, and control-plane nodes. You will see how routed access avoids spanning tree, how loopback addresses act as stable RLOCs for the overlay, and why choosing and configuring your underlay routing protocol correctly matters for scale and convergence. For example, assigning contiguous /32 loopbacks simplifies Router ID selection and route distribution, while using point-to-point links reduces OSPF complexity and speeds convergence. We will also show the CLI steps to configure loopbacks and OSPF and demonstrate verification commands that confirm your underlay is healthy. A common misconception is that overlay technologies can compensate for a poor underlay — they cannot; the overlay depends entirely on full IP reachability. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design loopback and link addressing, select and configure an underlay protocol, verify end-to-end RLOC reachability, and recognize configuration mistakes that break reachability. Takeaway: a well-designed underlay prevents many later troubleshooting headaches in the overlay.

These learning objectives will guide your hands-on work with an SD-Access underlay. First, you'll design an IP addressing scheme that separates loopbacks from point-to-point link subnets and follows best practice allocations so RLOCs remain stable. For example, reserving a /24 or larger contiguous block for loopbacks and using /30 links avoids address overlap and improves troubleshooting. Second, you'll configure a robust underlay routing protocol—OSPF, EIGRP, or ISIS—ensuring full reachability of loopback RLOCs. Knowing when to pick OSPF versus ISIS matters in scaling. Third, you'll implement routed access by extending Layer 3 to the access edge, which removes spanning tree complexity and shortens convergence. Finally, you'll learn to identify common pitfalls such as inconsistent area IDs, missing loopback advertisements, and accidentally extending Layer 2 across fabric edge nodes. Each objective includes verification steps and an example so you can practice with confidence.

These objectives focus on practical verification and the small design details that prevent outages. You will learn to verify underlay connectivity using OSPF neighbor tables, routing tables, pings to loopback addresses, and traceroutes to confirm forwarding paths. For addressing detail, you will practice assigning /32 loopbacks from a contiguous block and selecting /30 or /31 subnets for point-to-point links — including when unnumbered interfaces make sense. Additionally, you will apply the OSPF 'ip ospf network point-to-point' optimization on those links to prevent unnecessary DR/BDR elections and accelerate convergence. Each objective is paired with practical CLI steps so you can test and validate during hands-on labs. A good verification habit saves hours of troubleshooting later, and these skills are directly usable in real SD-Access underlay deployments. Learning Objectives — Practice & Verification means verification and careful addressing choices are as important as initial configuration for a stable underlay.. In practical terms, hands-on skills and verification you will master. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The underlay is the IP transport network that connects all fabric-enabled devices and provides the basic reachability the overlay requires. In SD-Access the underlay should be routed: that means every physical link between switches and routers is a Layer 3 point-to-point connection, and there is no Layer 2 stretching across multiple fabric edge nodes. Concretely, the underlay carries routes to the loopback addresses of every device, which act as RLOCs for the LISP overlay. A practical example: if an access switch needs to reach the control-plane node, it uses the underlay routes to the control-plane loopback IP. A common misconception is that overlay smartness replaces a solid underlay; it does not. The overlay relies on the underlay for IP reachability, and problems in the underlay show up as broken overlay services. Key reasons the underlay matters include faster convergence from routed access, elimination of STP limitations, and localized failure domains that reduce outage scope. When designing the underlay, plan addressing, choose an appropriate routing protocol, and confirm loopbacks and point-to-point links are advertised. Reflect: before touching the overlay, can you verify that every loopback is reachable from every fabric node?

Routed access and Layer 2 extension represent two very different underlay philosophies. Routed access extends Layer 3 to the access edge and treats each link as a point-to-point routed segment; Layer 2 extension stretches VLANs across devices and depends on Spanning Tree Protocol. Routed access is recommended for SD-Access because it eliminates STP complexity, localizes failure domains, and allows faster convergence. For example, if a link fails in a routed access design, only that subnet and adjacent routes reconverge, whereas a Layer 2 domain can trigger broader STP recalculations and longer reconvergence windows. A common mistake is attempting to maintain stretched VLANs to preserve legacy behavior; this reintroduces STP and undermines the overlay's separation of forwarding and control. The benefit in practice is stable, predictable underlay behavior that the overlay can depend on. Consider a campus where hundreds of access switches exist: routed access prevents a single broadcast domain from ballooning and causing widespread instability. Question to reflect on: if you inherit a network with VLANs stretched across access nodes, what steps will you take to migrate to routed access safely?

A deliberate IP addressing plan makes an SD-Access underlay manageable and scalable. Start by reserving a contiguous block for loopback interfaces — for example a /24 or /22 depending on fabric size — and assign /32 addresses to each device's loopback. These loopbacks become the RLOCs used by the overlay, and using contiguous addresses simplifies summarization and documentation. Next, allocate small subnets for point-to-point links, typically /30 or /31; these conserve address space and clearly indicate link endpoints. Where supported, you can use unnumbered interfaces to avoid wasting addresses, but be consistent and document the approach. A typical process: 1) Estimate number of fabric devices and select loopback block size; 2) Reserve a separate block for P2P links; 3) Assign static /32 loopbacks and small P2P subnets; 4) Update routing protocol advertisements and verify. Example: use 10.255.255.0/24 for loopbacks with 10.255.255.1 and.2 as device /32s, and 192.168.10.0/30 for a specific link. Misconception to avoid: using large shared subnets for access links that blur routing boundaries. The core question: does your address plan make it trivial to locate which subnet belongs to which link or device?

Loopback interfaces are virtual interfaces with a stable, always-up IP address, and in SD-Access they serve two critical roles. First, a loopback often becomes the Router ID for your routing protocol, ensuring a consistent identity even as physical interfaces flap. Second, loopback addresses serve as RLOCs — LISP Routing Locators — in the overlay control plane so that the overlay maps endpoints to physical devices. Best practice is to place loopbacks into a dedicated contiguous subnet and assign each device a /32. For instance, using 10.255.255.0/24 for all loopbacks and giving FabricEdge1 10.255.255.1/32 guarantees predictability. Several recurring mistakes cause underlay failures. First, extending Layer 2 across fabric edge nodes undermines routed access and reintroduces STP issues. Avoid this by migrating ports to routed interfaces and performing the overlay segmentation in software. Second, inconsistent routing protocol settings — such as wrong OSPF area IDs or incorrect EIGRP AS numbers — can prevent full adjacency or route propagation. Always standardize process IDs and area numbers in your design documents. Third, failing to advertise loopbacks into the routing process is a frequent source of missing RLOCs; verify network statements or redistribution policies. Fourth, careless addressing, such as using large shared subnets for links, can make it hard to determine endpoints and invite mistakes. Mitigation strategies include documenting address plans, applying configuration templates, performing changes in maintenance windows, and validating with show commands before overlay deployment. A useful practice is a pre-overlay checklist: verify loopback advertisements, confirm OSPF neighbors are Full, and ping every loopback from multiple nodes.
